content: Recombinant human activated protein C (rhAPC) is a substance with a wide range of effects on both coagulation and inflammation. While it has shown potential to reduce mortality in adults with sepsis, no significant benefits have been observed in pediatric populations with severe sepsis. The purpose of this study was to evaluate whether rhAPC could reduce mortality or morbidity in neonates with sepsis. Neonatal sepsis remains a significant clinical challenge, with high mortality rates despite a decline in its overall incidence. To investigate this, a comprehensive search was conducted in May 2011 across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, and others. The search also included doctoral dissertations, theses, and the Science Citation Index. No restrictions were placed on language. The focus was on randomized or quasi-randomized trials that compared rhAPC to placebo or no intervention as an adjunct to antibiotic therapy in neonates (both preterm and term) under 28 days of age with suspected or confirmed severe sepsis. Eligible studies were required to report at least one of the following outcomes: mortality during the initial hospital stay, neurodevelopmental outcomes at two years of age or later, length of hospital stay, duration of mechanical ventilation, chronic lung disease, periventricular leukomalacia, intraventricular hemorrhage, necrotizing enterocolitis, bleeding, or other adverse events. The review authors planned to independently assess the quality and inclusion criteria of the studies, extract relevant data, and resolve any disagreements through consensus. Statistical analyses were to include measures such as relative risk, risk difference, and number needed to treat for dichotomous outcomes, as well as weighted mean differences for continuous outcomes, all reported with 95% confidence intervals. A fixed-effect model was to be used for meta-analysis, and heterogeneity was to be assessed using the I² statistic. However, no eligible trials were identified during the search. Furthermore, in October 2011, Eli Lilly withdrew rhAPC (marketed as Xigris®) from the market after a clinical trial in adults demonstrated higher mortality rates associated with its use. As a result, Xigris® (DrotAA) is no longer recommended for use in any age group, and the product has been recalled. In conclusion, despite the theoretical justification for using rhAPC in neonatal sepsis, there is insufficient evidence to support its use in this population. The lack of efficacy observed in adults, combined with an increased risk of bleeding and the subsequent market withdrawal of rhAPC, indicates that it should not be used in neonates. Additionally, further clinical trials investigating rhAPC in this context are not recommended.
